lead: The Myhill‑Nerode theorem characterises regular languages. It can be used to prove that a language is regular or not regular by examining the number of equivalence classes.
prereq: You need: deterministic finite automata (Chapter 2.5) and the notion of an equivalence relation (Chapter 2.1).

blocks.text: Let L be a language over an alphabet Σ. For any two strings x and y in Σ* define x ≡L y if for every string z in Σ* the concatenation xz is in L exactly when yz is in L. This relation looks at the future extensions of x and y.

blocks.where: x, y are strings; z is any possible suffix; L is the language under study.

blocks.text: The relation ≡L is an equivalence relation. It partitions Σ* into disjoint classes called Myhill‑Nerode classes. All strings in the same class behave identically with respect to L.

items: Reflexive: x ≡L x for every x.
Symmetric: if x ≡L y then y ≡L x.
Transitive: if x ≡L y and y ≡L w then x ≡L w.

blocks.text: The theorem says: A language L is regular if and only if the equivalence relation ≡L has a finite number of equivalence classes.

items: If L is regular, a DFA that recognises L can be built with one state for each class.
If ≡L has finitely many classes, a DFA can be constructed by taking the classes as states and using the transition rule [x] --a--> [xa].

blocks.text: The theorem gives both a test for regularity and a recipe for the smallest possible DFA.

sections.h3: From equivalence classes to a minimal DFA

items: Compute the relation ≡L for the language of interest.
Group all strings that are equivalent into classes.
Create a DFA state for each class.
Make the start state the class containing the empty string ε.
Mark a state as accepting if its class contains at least one string in L.
Define the transition: from class [x] on symbol a go to class [xa].

blocks.text: The resulting DFA is minimal. No two distinct states can be merged because their classes differ in future behaviour.
The algorithm is often called the Myhill‑Nerode minimisation. It is equivalent to the table‑filling method taught earlier, but it gives a clear conceptual picture.

figure.caption: The three equivalence classes for the language of strings ending with 01. Notice the accent style on the class of the empty string and the live style on the class ending with a single 0.

spec.aria: Shows three equivalence classes for a language of strings ending with 01.

examples.question: Let Σ={0,1} and L = { w ∈ Σ* | w ends with the suffix 01 }. (a) List all Myhill‑Nerode equivalence classes of ≡L. (b) Draw the minimal DFA that recognises L using those classes.
steps: Step 1: The empty string ε does not end with 01. Its future extensions are determined only by the suffixes that will appear later.
Step 2: The string "0" ends with a single 0. Any further symbol can turn it into a string that ends with 01 (by adding a 1) or keep it ending with 0 (by adding 0).
Step 3: The string "01" already ends with 01, so every extension stays in L.
Step 4: No other distinct behaviour exists. Any string that does not end with 0 or 01 behaves like ε; any string that ends with 0 behaves like "0"; any string that ends with 01 behaves like "01".
Step 5: Therefore the three classes are [ε], [0], and [01].
Step 6: Create a DFA state for each class: q0 = [ε] (start), q1 = [0], q2 = [01] (accepting).
• From q0 on 0 go to q1 (suffix becomes 0).
• From q0 on 1 stay in q0 (suffix still not 0).
• From q1 on 0 stay in q1 (suffix still 0).
• From q1 on 1 go to q2 (suffix becomes 01).
• From q2 on 0 go to q1 (suffix becomes 0).
• From q2 on 1 go to q0 (the resulting suffix does not end with 0 or 01, so it belongs to class [ε]).
Step 8: The DFA has three states and recognises exactly L.
examples.answer: The language L has three Myhill‑Nerode classes: [ε], [0] and [01]. The minimal DFA has three states with transitions as described above.

traps: Assuming that two strings with different prefixes must belong to different classes; only the suffix that determines future acceptance matters.
Treating the empty string ε as an accepting state because it is a suffix of every string; ε is accepting only if ε ∈ L, which is false here.
Confusing the transition from the accepting state on input 1; the correct target is the class [ε], not a new accepting state.
Counting the number of DFA states before minimisation; the theorem counts equivalence classes after minimisation.

quiz.q: What is the definition of the Myhill‑Nerode relation ≡L?
quiz.a: x ≡L y ⇔ for all strings z, xz ∈ L ↔ yz ∈ L.

quiz.q: Why does a finite number of ≡L classes guarantee that L is regular?
quiz.a: Each class can be used as a DFA state. With finitely many states the DFA recognises L, proving regularity.

quiz.q: Given Σ={a,b} and L = { w | w contains the substring aa }, list the Myhill‑Nerode classes.
quiz.a: [no a seen] – strings that have not yet seen the substring aa and whose last symbol is not a (i.e., end with b or are empty), [last symbol a] – strings that end with a but have not yet seen aa, [aa seen] – strings that already contain aa.

quiz.q: Construct the minimal DFA for the language of strings ending with 01 using the classes from the example.
quiz.a: Three states q0 ([ε]), q1 ([0]), q2 ([01]). Transitions: q0‑0→q1, q0‑1→q0, q1‑0→q1, q1‑1→q2, q2‑0→q1, q2‑1→q0. q2 is accepting.

quiz.q: If a DFA has 5 states but the Myhill‑Nerode theorem yields only 3 equivalence classes for its language, what can be concluded?
quiz.a: The DFA is not minimal; at least two states belong to the same equivalence class and can be merged.

quiz.q: Explain how the table‑filling algorithm and the Myhill‑Nerode approach produce the same minimal DFA.
quiz.a: Both methods identify indistinguishable states. Table‑filling marks pairs that can be merged; Myhill‑Nerode groups strings with identical future behaviour. The resulting partitions are identical, leading to the same minimal DFA.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the theorem underlies regex engine optimisations where a pattern is compiled to a minimal DFA for fast matching. Research uses Myhill‑Nerode concepts to study state complexity of language operations. Extensions appear in learning algorithms that infer minimal automata from examples. To explore further, search for "automata learning" and "state minimisation for weighted automata".
